title: Is ‘Aggressive Suicide’ the Next Social Contagion?
author: Gabriel Rossman
content:
![Is ‘Aggressive Suicide’ the Next Social
Contagion?](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-24-at-8.50.12
---PM-1.png)

Since Jason Arday's death, there has been a great deal of discussion about why
the institutions that had promoted and rewarded him showed such credulity
about the integrity of his work and plausibility of his biographical claims.
In what follows, I will put aside questions about Arday's rise to focus on how
he fell. Although his education and contributions, such as they were, were in
other fields, his last job title had "sociology" in it, and sociology has a
lot to say about the causes and consequences of his disgrace and death.

In his 2008 book _On Scandal_ , sociologist Ari Adut shows that scandal is
less about transgression than accusation. Even widespread shared knowledge of
a transgression spread by gossip is insufficient to create scandal until a
public accusation creates public knowledge of the relevant behavior and its
violation of a generally accepted moral code. The relevant audience might have
known of the transgression but can choose to ignore it until an accuser
obliges the audience to take a position on it. However, the accuser may also
face a backlash, especially if the accused's supporters find it easier to
emphasize the accuser's harassment than to defend the accused's behavior.

Adut's most vivid example is Oscar Wilde. The Victorians weren't so naive as
to understand Wilde as a man who directed his sexual attention solely to
women, but it was awkward to broach the subject, especially given that Wilde
was a beloved bon vivant. Shared knowledge of Wilde's sexuality turned into
scandalous public knowledge when the Marquess of Queensberry took revenge on
the writer, whom he blamed for corrupting his son, by leaving a calling card
addressed to "Oscar Wilde, posing sodomite." Wilde took the bait and sued
Queensberry for libel, but Queensberry had private detectives who were
prepared to back up the accusation.
